piezas.titulo: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum
piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. For more information about the Greenwood Village, Colorado clinic, visit http://www.spdSTAR.org or call 303-221-7827. About T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades): T.A.C.T is a 501(c)(3) that provides trade and technical skills to children, young adults and families living with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Early vocational training helps young adults before they leave high school and sets them up for long term success. Our programs are designed to empower individuals and develop interests and skills for life. To learn more visit: https://tactkids.org or call 720-460-0897. About Developmental Pathways: Developmental Pathways is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit agency serving individuals with developmental disabilities/delays and their families. We are also one of Colorado’s Community Centered Boards (CCB) connecting people to federal, state, county, and private funding in Arapahoe County, Douglas County, and the City of Aurora. We passionately believe inclusion is for everyone and offer services through Home and Community Based Medicaid Waiver programs, locally funded programs, and partnerships with other community organizations. To learn more visit: http://www.dpcolo.org by STAR Institute for SPD Sensory Processing Disorder

piezas.titulo: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
piezas.resumenOriginal: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). piezas.titulo: Penetrating needling from Qiuxu (GB40) to Zhaohai (KI6) versus separate needling for post-stroke lower-limb motor dysfunction: an assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial protocol
piezas.resumenOriginal: Post-stroke lower-limb motor dysfunction limits mobility, balance, and independence and remains a major target of neurorehabilitation. Acupuncture is widely used as an adjunctive intervention after stroke, but direct randomized evidence comparing penetrating needling with conventional separate needling at the same acupoints is limited. This protocol describes an active-comparator randomized controlled trial comparing penetrating needling from Qiuxu (GB40) to Zhaohai (KI6) with separate needling for post-stroke lower-limb motor dysfunction, with functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and surface electromyography (sEMG) included as exploratory mechanistic outcomes. This single-center, prospective, assessor-blinded, parallel-group superiority trial will enroll 130 participants with subacute post-stroke lower-limb motor dysfunction. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to penetrating needling from Qiuxu (GB40) to Zhaohai (KI6) or to separate needling at the same acupoints. Both groups will receive 12 acupuncture sessions over 2 weeks, delivered 6 times per week, with 30 min of needle retention per session, together with the same total rehabilitation dose of 30 min/day, 5 days/week. The primary outcome is the Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Lower Extremity (FMA-LE) score at the end of treatment (T1). The primary analysis will use analysis of covariance adjusted for baseline FMA-LE. Secondary clinical outcomes include the Berg Balance Scale, Manual Muscle Testing, and Modified Ashworth Scale. Registered secondary neurophysiological assessments include fNIRS and sEMG; their derived measures will be analyzed exploratorily.Clinical trial registrationhttps://itmctr.ccebtcm.org.cn/mgt/project/view/2037483478790045696, ITMCTR2026000773.

piezas.titulo: State-dependent responses of emotional brain networks in high myopia under blurred vision: a shift towards dorsal stream and cross-modal processing
piezas.resumenOriginal: PurposeReliable sensory input plays a vital role in shaping emotional experience, however, how the brain modulates the formation of emotion under chronic visual degradation remains unclear. Using high myopia (HM) as a natural model of sustained blur, this study investigated state-dependent responses of emotional brain networks during blurred movie viewing.MethodsTwenty-four participants with high myopia (HM) were tested without optical correction, comparing with normal vision (NV) controls from previous research. All participants watched thriller and scenic movie clips twice over one week during fMRI. Intra-subject synchrony and seed-based functional connectivity analyses focused on the amygdala and visual processing streams.ResultsCompared to NV controls, the HM group exhibited reduced intra-subject synchrony in visual cortices but increased synchrony in the primary auditory cortex, indicating cross-modal compensatory enhancement. During threat processing, HM participants showed strengthened and stable functional connectivity between the amygdala and the dorsal visual stream. For non-threatening content, this enhanced connectivity initially involved both dorsal and ventral stream but persisted selectively in the dorsal stream upon repeated viewing.ConclusionSustained visual blur elicits a perceptual-state-dependent functional response in emotional networks, characterized by heightened cross-modal auditory integration and an increased recruitment of the visual dorsal stream during blurred viewing. These findings highlight the brain’s immediate compensatory mechanisms under conditions of ambiguous visual input.

piezas.titulo: Data Integration Landscape 2026: Event Streaming, API, and Batch in the Era of Agentic AI
piezas.resumenOriginal: Data integration used to be treated as back-office plumbing. Difficult, yes, and always operationally critical, but rarely seen as strategic. That has changed. The Data Integration Landscape 2026 maps this shift across three communication paradigms and every major vendor. The largest software companies in the world have paid a fortune to own the integration layer: IBM acquired Confluent for $11 billion, Salesforce acquired Informatica for $8 billion, Qlik absorbed Talend, TIBCO folded into Cloud Software Group, and Fivetran merged with dbt Labs. When integration vendors command prices like these, the integration layer has become a strategic asset, not a piece of infrastructure to take for granted. The pressure behind this has been building for a long time. Data volumes keep exploding, digitalization keeps pushing more of the business onto real-time rails, and the demand for fresh data has been rising for years. AI is the latest and most acute driver. Models and autonomous agents need data that is current, governed, and continuously flowing. A nightly batch job and an API that returns yesterday's state cannot support a system making decisions in the moment. An agent working from outdated data does not fail loudly. It confidently does the wrong thing. That raised the stakes on a problem enterprises have been wrestling with for a decade.

piezas.titulo: Amygdala Persistence in Aging: Replication and Extension of Puccetti et al. (2021)
piezas.resumenOriginal: Age-related differences in affect are well established, but their neural mechanisms remain unclear. In a preregistered replication of Puccetti et al. (2021) and extension, we examined age, affect, left-amygdala negative persistence, and amygdala-ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) task-based connectivity using MIDUS 3 daily diary and fMRI data. Older age predicted higher positive and lower negative affect in the daily diary sample (N = 1,168; ps < .001). In the primary diary + fMRI sample (N = 81; ages 48-95, 61.7% female, 82.7% White), greater persistence predicted higher raw negative affect ({beta} = 0.278, 95% CI [0.012, 0.544], p = .020); associations with positive and log-transformed negative affect were nonsignificant (ps [≥] .063). Older age predicted lower persistence in the final fMRI sample (N = 127; {beta} = -0.00260, 95% CI [-0.00504, -0.00016], p = .018), but this association was weaker in the primary diary + fMRI sample (p = .200), with no evidence of mediation. Greater anterior vmPFC connectivity predicted lower raw negative affect ({beta} = -0.106, 95% CI [-0.223, 0.012], p = .039) and log-transformed negative affect (p = .014). In MIDUS Refresher 1, affect estimates were directionally similar but nonsignificant (N = 48; ps [≥] .081), whereas the age-persistence estimate reversed direction. These findings provide partial support for amygdala persistence and task-based connectivity as neural correlates of daily affect, while highlighting variability in the magnitude and replicability of fMRI-behavior associations.

piezas.titulo: Peer Mentoring Benefits in Rehabilitation for Individuals With Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Importance The lived experiences of peer mentors with spinal cord injury (SCI) provide distinct value in the rehabilitation process and contribute to improved outcomes. When combined with traditional therapy, peer mentorship programs can enhance life satisfaction among individuals living with SCI. Objective To explore the impact that peer-led mentorship programs and interventions have on the rehabilitation outcomes for individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI). Data sources PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MedNar, and OpenGrey were searched between 2014 and 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was adapted and used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. Study selection and data collection Inclusion criteria included individuals with SCI who participated in peer mentorship and reported outcomes on quality of life, well-being, independence, or activities of daily living (ADLs) or instrumental ADLs. Exclusion criteria included interventions conducted via telehealth or reported outcomes of social participation. Findings Five articles were analyzed for synthesis, which included individuals 18 yr and older with an SCI. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Findings may have limited generalizability across different settings and populations because of the small number of available studies and variability in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures. None of the articles reviewed included occupational therapists. Conclusions and relevance This review highlighted the benefits of peer mentorship in enhanced life satisfaction. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Future research should examine the benefits of incorporating peer-led intervention programs across the continuum of care, including occupational therapy, in enhancing best practices in SCI rehabilitation. Plain-Language Summary: Peer mentorship programs can help people with spinal cord injuries adjust to daily life by providing guidance, support, and encouragement that professionals without lived experience may not offer. This review found that peer mentoring can improve psychological well-being and health management and reduce unplanned hospital visits. Evidence is limited because of the small number of studies and variations in study design; however, the results suggest that meaningful benefits may be present. Further research is needed to determine the most effective way to implement peer mentorship across rehabilitation settings.

piezas.titulo: Intrinsic circadian organization of the spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Introduction Circadian rhythms coordinate daily fluctuations in physiology and behavior, yet their organization within primary sensory pathways remains poorly defined. Although somatosensory responsiveness varies across the day-night cycle, it is unclear whether peripheral sensory circuits possess molecular mechanisms for temporal regulation. Objectives To determine whether the spinal-peripheral sensory axis harbors intrinsic circadian clocks and to define the molecular scope and functional organization of circadian regulation in dorsal root ganglia (DRGs). Methods We used real-time bioluminescence imaging to assess circadian oscillations of the core clock protein PER2 in the spinal dorsal horn and DRGs. To characterize molecular regulation, we performed RNA sequencing across a 52-hour circadian time course in DRGs. Results We demonstrate that the spinal dorsal horn and DRGs harbor robust, tissue-autonomous circadian clocks, with sustained PER2 oscillations. Circadian analysis identified 626 rhythmic genes (3.6% of expressed genes) in DRGs, with nonuniform phase distributions forming discrete temporal clusters. Functional annotation revealed phase-specific enrichment of processes including transport, neuronal structure, and proteostasis, suggesting coordinated temporal deployment of distinct molecular programs rather than uniform oscillations. Cross-referencing with neuropathic pain-associated genes revealed limited overlap; however, overlapping genes aligned to specific baseline phase windows enriched for regenerative annotations. Potassium channel-related signaling components implicated in neuropathic pain also showed baseline circadian modulation. Conclusion These findings establish the spinal dorsal horn and DRGs as intrinsically circadian tissues and reveal a temporally structured molecular landscape in DRG, providing a framework for understanding how peripheral sensory processing, plasticity, and homeostatic regulation are coordinated across the day-night cycle.
